rejected.title: Discussing different readings
card: A moment in a text can often be read in more than one way. Writers may leave room for different responses.
Show you see this with phrases such as "on one reading" or "alternatively". Then explain the other reading fairly.
Next, argue for the reading you find more convincing. Give a reason based on the text, such as its language or its context.
Do not just list readings and stop, or call them all equally valid. Do not invent a reading that the text cannot support.
rejected.remember: Offer more than one reading, then argue for one using the text.

a.q: In an invented story, a girl leaves her home town at night without a word. What is the strongest way to discuss this moment?
opts: Give two readings, then argue for one using the text
Give one reading and say no other is possible
Give several readings, then end without choosing one
Say readers disagree, so the moment has no meaning
a.why: Naming two readings and then arguing for one with evidence from the text shows depth. Listing several readings without choosing one is tempting, but it leaves the argument unfinished.
a.clue: Noticing other readings is not the whole task.

b.q: A student writes that the ending can be read as hopeful, and that another reader might find it bleak. What should the student add to show depth?
opts: A reason from the text for preferring one reading
A third reading that has no support in the text
A claim that both readings are equally correct
A summary of the plot before the ending
b.why: The student has named two readings but has not argued for either. A reason from the text turns a list into an argument. Saying both are equally correct avoids taking a position.
b.clue: Naming readings is only half the task.
